title: Vayelech: the hidden face (Deuteronomy 31:17–18)
hook: the Torah foresees times when God's face seems hidden

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last commandment: write this song. Your line was write your own. Today, a hard verse from the same chapter.

There's a silence that comes after you pray, or hope, or ask, and nothing answers. In a hospital waiting room, or at three in the morning. The Psalms give it words: a voice asking how long God will hide His face. To some it feels like the opposite of what faith promised. What's surprising is that the Torah itself sees this silence coming. Before the people even cross the river, God tells Moses there will be times like this.
screen: `AFTER THE ASKING, SILENCE.` → `HOW LONG WILT THOU HIDE?` → `THE TORAH SEES IT COMING.`

segments.voice: God tells Moses that in time the people will stray, and troubles will find them. Then: "And I will surely hide My face in that day." In Hebrew, haster astir panai. From it comes a phrase Jewish thought keeps returning to: hester panim, the hiding of the face. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say God leaves, or stops existing, or stops caring. A face that's hidden is still there. And the verse lets the people speak their pain: are not these evils come upon us, they ask, because our God is not among us? The text puts that feeling into words. It doesn't pretend the silence is easy. The rabbis found a quiet surprise inside the Hebrew. The Talmud, in Chullin, asks where the book of Esther is hinted at in the Torah, and answers with this verse: haster astir, I will surely hide. Esther. It's a book of the Bible in which God is never named, and yet its story turns, again and again, at just the right moment. Hidden, the rabbis suggest, isn't the same as absent. After the Holocaust, some Jewish thinkers reached for hester panim to name what had happened. Others found even that phrase too small, or refused any explanation at all. Both responses live inside the tradition. What the verse offers is permission to name the silence honestly, without calling it the end.
screen: `HASTER ASTIR: I WILL HIDE.` · `A HIDDEN FACE IS STILL THERE.` · `ESTHER: GOD NEVER NAMED.` · `NAMING THE SILENCE HONESTLY.` · then, large: `HIDDEN, NOT GONE.`

segments.voice: Don't fill the quiet: if there's something you've asked for or hoped for that hasn't come, let it be there, without explaining it or defending anyone. If you pray, you can bring the psalm's old question, how long, and let it stand without an answer; if you don't, sit with the quiet as it is, and notice that you're still here inside it.
Hester panim. The hiding of the face. A silence the Torah foresaw, and called hidden, not gone.
Your line: hidden, not gone. A hidden face is still there. That's day five hundred twenty-six.

screen: `DAY 526 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HA'AZINU: GIVE EAR, O HEAVENS (DEUTERONOMY 32:1).`

howItsDone: Hester panim is an idea Jewish thinkers turn to when reflecting on suffering and divine silence, and the book of Esther, read on Purim, is often taught alongside it: a story in which God is never named.
